summary: C458 Health, Fitness, and Wellness (4 CUs) is a general-education course on the foundations of good health, with extra attention to children and adolescents: mental, emotional and social wellness, social and emotional learning, disease, fitness and lifestyle, nutrition, and substance use. You pass one proctored objective assessment whose length and passing score WGU doesn't publish, and no readable student reports were available for this guide, so its difficulty is unknown. Federal nutrition advice changed in January 2026, so learn the numbers from both the 2025–2030 and 2020–2025 Dietary Guidelines, and treat this guide as study material, not medical advice.
author: Dorian Acosta

assessment.format: One proctored OA · question count, time limit and passing score not published · online proctoring through Meazure Learning and the Guardian Browser
details: Assessment: one objective assessment (OA), a proctored exam. WGU's public pages don't give the question count, time limit, question types or passing score. No student report with those numbers was available for this guide, so check the assessment page in the course before you schedule it.

What it covers (official): four competencies: what shapes mental, emotional and social wellness; the core competencies of social and emotional learning; how disease, fitness and lifestyle affect the body; and nutrition and a healthy diet. The course description adds health, nutrition, fitness and substance use and abuse, with a focus on children and adolescents.

Guideline versions: USDA and HHS replaced the 2020–2025 Dietary Guidelines with a 2025–2030 edition in January 2026. The new edition introduces a food pyramid graphic (the 2020–2025 edition used MyPlate) and replaces the 10%-of-calories added-sugar limit with advice that no amount of added sugar is recommended and no meal should have more than 10 grams. Course materials often lag new guidelines, so the OA may still use the older numbers. This guide gives both wherever they differ.

Proctoring rules (official): WGU's catalog requires your own personal (not work or school) computer running Windows 10+ or macOS 13 Ventura+ for proctored online OAs. Chrome OS, Linux, Windows on Arm (including Snapdragon laptops), Windows in S Mode, virtual machines, and phones or tablets running iOS, iPadOS or Android aren't allowed. You also need the Guardian Browser, one monitor, an external webcam that's elevated to give the required viewing angle (a laptop's built-in camera doesn't meet the requirement), speakers instead of headphones, and a personal rather than work or public network. You may not use unapproved materials or read questions aloud, you must stay in view with your hands and arms visible, and WGU may record the session.

Course facts: 4 CUs, term 1 of the BSCS standard path (catalog 202611; WGU's catalog lists it as HLTH 1010). Many WGU programs share it as a general-education course, so ask about transfer credit if you've already taken a college health or nutrition course.
Deadline (official): a course you haven't passed by the end of the term, including one you never attempted, is recorded as Not Passed and counts against satisfactory academic progress.
tips: Study by competency. Wellness and SEL are topics 1–4 here, disease, fitness and lifestyle are topics 5–6 and 10–12, and nutrition is topics 7–9.
Ask your instructor which Dietary Guidelines edition the course materials follow, and learn both sets of numbers until you know.
Build a one-page numbers sheet: activity minutes and sleep hours by age, calories per gram, AMDRs, BMI cutoffs, blood pressure and A1C ranges, sodium limits and the standard drink.
Practice matching behaviors to the CASEL competencies and to the stages of change. Neighboring competencies and stages sound alike, so name the exact skill or stage a behavior shows.
Read the age group in every question: children, teens and adults have different activity, sleep, sodium and BMI rules.
If the course has a pre-assessment, use it as a readiness check and study the weak competencies it reports, not just the score.
Testing at home: set up an elevated external webcam and speakers, close other programs, and run WGU's System Check on the exam computer a few days before.

competencies: Course planning: discuss your course planning tool report with your instructor and build a personalized course plan together.
The graduate identifies factors that influence mental, emotional, and social wellness.
The graduate identifies the application of the core competencies of social and emotional learning.
The graduate identifies the influence of disease, fitness, and lifestyle on the body.
The graduate identifies the principles of nutrition and the components of a healthy diet.

topics.title: Wellness, the determinants of health and changing a behavior
topics.eli5: Health isn't just not being sick. It's how well your body, mind, relationships and surroundings work together, and much of it comes from daily habits you can change one step at a time.
topics.detail: The World Health Organization's classic definition calls health a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease, and wellness is the active process of making choices toward it. SAMHSA's model lists eight dimensions of wellness: emotional, environmental, financial, intellectual, occupational, physical, social and spiritual. Textbooks often use six or seven, so learn your course's list. Health is shaped by factors you can't change (age, genes, sex, family history), by behaviors you can (activity, diet, sleep, substance use) and by social determinants of health. Healthy People 2030 defines those as the conditions where people are born, live, learn, work, play, worship and age, grouped into five domains: economic stability, education access and quality, health care access and quality, neighborhood and built environment, and social and community context. Behavior change rarely happens all at once. The transtheoretical (stages of change) model describes precontemplation (not intending to change in the next six months), contemplation (thinking about changing within about six months), preparation (planning to act soon, usually within a month), action (changed recently) and maintenance (kept the change for six months or more). SMART goals (specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound), self-monitoring, social support and small rewards help people move forward, and a relapse is treated as part of the process rather than a failure.
points: SAMHSA's 8 dimensions: emotional, environmental, financial, intellectual, occupational, physical, social, spiritual
Healthy People 2030's 5 social-determinant domains: economic stability · education · health care · neighborhood and built environment · social and community context
Stages of change: precontemplation → contemplation → preparation → action → maintenance
Modifiable risk factors (diet, activity, tobacco, alcohol, sleep) vs non-modifiable ones (age, genes, family history)
SMART goal example: walk briskly for 20 minutes after dinner on 5 days a week for the next 4 weeks

topics.title: Mental and emotional health, stress and sleep
topics.eli5: Stress is your body's alarm system. A little helps you rise to a challenge, but an alarm that never switches off wears down your body and your mood.
topics.detail: Mental and emotional wellness depends on biological factors (genes, brain chemistry, illness, sleep), psychological factors (coping skills, self-esteem, past trauma) and social and environmental factors (relationships, school or work pressure, poverty, discrimination, social media and adverse childhood experiences). NIMH describes stress as the body's physical or mental response to an outside cause, while anxiety can continue even without a real threat. The fight-or-flight response releases adrenaline (epinephrine) and cortisol, which raise heart rate, blood pressure and blood sugar. Hans Selye's general adaptation syndrome describes three stages of prolonged stress: alarm, resistance and exhaustion. Short-term stress can help (eustress, such as getting ready for a game or a presentation), but chronic distress is linked to poor sleep, weaker immunity, digestive and heart problems, anxiety and depression. Healthy coping includes exercise, sleep, time management, relaxation and mindfulness, journaling, challenging unhelpful thoughts, cutting back on caffeine and talking with supportive people or a professional. Unhealthy coping includes substance use, avoidance and self-harm. Youth mental health is a major concern: in CDC's 2025 Youth Risk Behavior Survey, 33% of high school students reported persistent sadness or hopelessness (43% of girls, 24% of boys), down from about 40% in 2023, and 14% had seriously considered suicide. Anyone in crisis can call or text 988, the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. Sleep supports all of this: CDC recommends 9–12 hours for ages 6–12, 8–10 for teens 13–17 and 7 or more for adults 18–60.
points: Eustress (helpful, short-term) vs distress (harmful, especially when it's chronic)
General adaptation syndrome: alarm → resistance → exhaustion
Stress hormones: adrenaline (epinephrine) and cortisol
Warning signs to act on: withdrawal, big changes in sleep or appetite, hopelessness, talk of self-harm; call or text 988
Sleep hygiene: a consistent schedule, screens off 30+ minutes before bed, no caffeine late in the day, a cool and quiet room

topics.title: Social and emotional learning: the CASEL 5
topics.eli5: SEL is learning the people skills: knowing your feelings, handling them, understanding others, getting along and making good choices.
topics.detail: The second competency covers social and emotional learning (SEL). CASEL (the Collaborative for Academic, Social, and Emotional Learning) describes SEL as how people of all ages learn and use the skills to build a healthy identity, manage emotions, reach goals, feel and show empathy, keep supportive relationships and make responsible, caring decisions. Its framework names five core competencies. Self-awareness is understanding your own emotions, thoughts and values and how they affect your behavior, such as naming a feeling, knowing your strengths and believing you can grow. Self-management is regulating your emotions, thoughts and actions to reach goals, such as handling stress, controlling impulses and staying motivated. Social awareness is understanding other people's perspectives and feeling empathy, including for people from different backgrounds. Relationship skills are building and keeping healthy relationships: communicating clearly, listening, cooperating, resolving conflict constructively, resisting negative social pressure, and asking for or offering help. Responsible decision-making is making caring, constructive choices by weighing ethics, safety and the consequences for yourself and others. CASEL's wheel places these competencies inside four settings where they're taught and practiced: classrooms, schools, families and caregivers, and communities. SEL ties directly to health: self-management helps with stress and impulse control, and relationship skills help young people resist negative peer pressure and protect against bullying and isolation.
points: Self-awareness: "I get anxious before tests, and I know I'm good at explaining things"
Self-management: taking slow breaths and counting to ten before answering an angry text
Social awareness: noticing a new classmate eating alone and imagining how they feel
Relationship skills: using an "I" statement, agreeing on a compromise, or saying no when friends pressure you to vape
Responsible decision-making: weighing the consequences and refusing a ride from a driver who has been drinking
Settings: classrooms, schools, families and caregivers, communities

topics.title: Social wellness, relationships and bullying
topics.eli5: Good relationships are a safety net. People who listen, respect your limits and have your back make every other part of health easier.
topics.detail: Social wellness means having supportive relationships and a sense of belonging. Loneliness and social isolation are linked to depression, heart disease and earlier death, and connection to family, school and community protects young people's health. Healthy relationships have respect, trust, honesty, support, fairness and good communication, while unhealthy ones involve control, jealousy, cutting someone off from friends, put-downs or violence. Communication style matters. Assertive communication states your needs clearly and respectfully, often with an "I" statement such as "I feel frustrated when plans change at the last minute." Passive communication hides your needs, and aggressive communication attacks the other person. Conflict resolution usually means calming down, listening to understand, describing the problem without blame, brainstorming solutions and agreeing on one. CDC defines bullying as unwanted aggressive behavior that involves a real or perceived power imbalance and is repeated, or likely to be repeated. It can be physical, verbal, relational (exclusion, rumors) or online (cyberbullying), and bystanders who report it or support the target can stop it. Peer pressure can be negative or positive, and refusal skills (say no clearly, give a reason, suggest something else, leave) help young people avoid risky behavior.
points: Assertive (clear and respectful) vs passive (hides needs) vs aggressive (hostile)
"I" statement pattern: I feel ___ when ___ because ___, and I'd like ___
Bullying = unwanted aggression + power imbalance + repetition; cyberbullying can follow a child home at any hour
Warning signs of an unhealthy relationship: control, jealousy, isolation from friends, threats
Refusal skills: say no, give a reason, offer an alternative, walk away

topics.title: Physical activity guidelines by age
topics.eli5: Kids need about an hour of moving every day. Adults need about two and a half hours a week, plus some muscle work.
topics.detail: The Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans (2nd edition, HHS, 2018) are still the current federal guidelines. HHS took public comments in fall 2026 for a supplement on step counts and muscle-strengthening that's due in 2027. Preschool children (ages 3–5) should be active throughout the day with active play of any intensity, about 3 hours a day. Children and adolescents (6–17) need 60 minutes or more of moderate-to-vigorous activity every day, mostly aerobic, including vigorous activity on at least 3 days a week, muscle-strengthening (climbing, push-ups) on at least 3 days and bone-strengthening (jumping, running) on at least 3 days. Adults need 150–300 minutes a week of moderate-intensity aerobic activity, or 75–150 minutes of vigorous activity, or an equivalent combination of the two (1 vigorous minute counts about the same as 2 moderate minutes). They also need muscle-strengthening for all major muscle groups on 2 or more days. Older adults aim for the adult amounts as their abilities allow and add multicomponent activity that includes balance training. Healthy pregnant and postpartum women should get at least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity a week and ask their doctor whether or how to adjust their activity. The 2nd edition dropped the old rule that only bouts of 10 minutes or more count: any activity counts, and adults should move more and sit less. Benefits include lower risk of heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, several cancers, depression and dementia, plus immediate gains in mood, sleep, blood pressure and insulin sensitivity. For children, activity also builds bone, fitness and attention.
points: Ages 3–5: active all day, about 3 hours of play at any intensity
Ages 6–17: 60+ minutes daily, with vigorous, muscle-strengthening and bone-strengthening activity each on 3+ days a week
Adults: 150–300 min moderate or 75–150 min vigorous per week, plus muscle-strengthening on 2+ days
Older adults: add balance and multicomponent activity · pregnancy and postpartum: 150+ min moderate
Bouts of any length count, and sitting less matters too

topics.title: Fitness components, training principles and intensity
topics.eli5: Fitness has parts: heart and lungs, strength, endurance, flexibility and body makeup. Each one improves only when you train it a little harder than it's used to.
topics.detail: Health-related fitness has five components. Cardiorespiratory endurance is how well the heart, lungs and blood vessels deliver oxygen during sustained activity. Muscular strength is the most force a muscle can produce, and muscular endurance is how long it can repeat or hold an effort. Flexibility is the range of motion at a joint, and body composition is the proportion of fat to lean mass. Skill-related fitness adds agility, balance, coordination, power, reaction time and speed, which matter most for sports. The FITT principle describes a workout: frequency (how often), intensity (how hard), time (how long) and type (what kind). Training follows overload (doing more than the body is used to), progression (increasing the load gradually), specificity (you improve what you train), reversibility (fitness fades when you stop) and individual differences. Intensity can be measured three ways. Absolute intensity uses METs: 1 MET is the energy you use sitting at rest, moderate activity is 3.0–5.9 METs and vigorous is 6.0 or more. Relative intensity uses a 0–10 effort scale, where moderate is 5–6 and vigorous starts at about 7–8, or the talk test: during moderate activity you can talk but not sing, and during vigorous activity you can say only a few words before pausing for breath. Heart rate is the third gauge. The American Heart Association estimates maximum heart rate as about 220 minus your age, with a target of roughly 50–70% of maximum for moderate exercise and 70–85% for vigorous. These figures are averages, and some medicines lower heart rate, so people who have a heart condition or take medication should ask a health care professional for their own target. Other sources use slightly different percentages, so use whichever method your course teaches. Every session should start with a warm-up and end with a cool-down, and rest days let muscles repair and adapt.
points: Health-related components: cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility, body composition
FITT: frequency, intensity, time, type
Training principles: overload, progression, specificity, reversibility, individuality
Max heart rate ≈ 220 − age. At age 40 that's about 180 bpm, so moderate ≈ 90–126 bpm and vigorous ≈ 126–153 bpm
Moderate: brisk walking (2.5 mph or faster), doubles tennis, recreational swimming · vigorous: jogging or running, lap swimming, singles tennis, jumping rope

topics.title: Nutrients: macronutrients, micronutrients and water
topics.eli5: Food gives you fuel (carbs, fat and protein), building blocks (protein and minerals) and tiny helpers (vitamins), and water carries everything around.
topics.detail: The six classes of nutrients are carbohydrates, proteins, fats (lipids), vitamins, minerals and water. The first three are macronutrients that supply energy: carbohydrate and protein give about 4 calories per gram and fat about 9. Alcohol, which isn't a nutrient, gives about 7. Carbohydrates are the body's main energy source and come as simple sugars or as complex starches and fiber. Fiber aids digestion and helps control blood sugar and cholesterol, and the 2020–2025 Dietary Guidelines set fiber goals at 14 grams per 1,000 calories. Proteins are built from amino acids, nine of which are essential because the body can't make them. Complete proteins, from animal foods and soy, contain all nine. Fats supply energy, insulate the body and carry the fat-soluble vitamins. Unsaturated fats (olive oil, nuts, fish rich in omega-3s) are linked to better heart health, saturated fats (butter, fatty meats, full-fat dairy, coconut oil) raise LDL cholesterol, and artificial trans fats have been largely removed from U.S. foods. The Acceptable Macronutrient Distribution Ranges for adults are 45–65% of calories from carbohydrate, 20–35% from fat and 10–35% from protein. Young children need a larger share from fat: 30–40% at ages 1–3 and 25–35% from 4 to 18. Vitamins are either fat-soluble (A, D, E and K, stored in the body, so high-dose supplements can build up to harmful levels) or water-soluble (vitamin C and the B vitamins, which you need regularly). Key minerals include calcium, which with vitamin D builds bone (most peak bone mass is built in adolescence), and iron, which carries oxygen in the blood (a shortage causes anemia, and teen girls need more). Sodium and potassium control fluid balance and blood pressure. Water makes up more than half of body weight and regulates temperature, so water and unsweetened drinks are the best choices.
points: Calories per gram: carbohydrate 4 · protein 4 · fat 9 · alcohol 7
Adult AMDRs: carbohydrate 45–65% · fat 20–35% · protein 10–35%
Fat-soluble vitamins: A, D, E, K · water-soluble: vitamin C and the B vitamins
Bones: calcium + vitamin D · blood: iron · blood pressure: less sodium, more potassium
Worked example: 10 g fat + 30 g carbohydrate + 5 g protein = 90 + 120 + 20 = 230 calories

topics.title: The Dietary Guidelines: 2025–2030 vs 2020–2025, and food labels
topics.eli5: The government's healthy-eating advice changed in January 2026: eat mostly real, minimally processed food, put protein and produce first, and skip added sugar.
topics.detail: USDA and HHS update the Dietary Guidelines for Americans every five years. The 2025–2030 edition, released in January 2026, is built around one message, "eat real food": choose whole, nutrient-dense foods (protein, dairy, vegetables, fruits, healthy fats and whole grains) and sharply limit highly processed foods. It sets protein at 1.2–1.6 grams per kilogram of body weight per day and whole grains at 2–4 servings a day, and for a 2,000-calorie pattern it sets 3 servings of dairy (full-fat dairy with no added sugars is encouraged), 3 servings of vegetables and 2 of fruit, with every goal adjusted to a person's calorie needs. Saturated fat should stay at or below 10% of daily calories. No amount of added sugar or non-nutritive sweetener is recommended, and no single meal should have more than 10 grams of added sugar. Sodium should stay below 2,300 mg a day from age 14, with lower limits for children: under 1,200 mg at ages 1–3, 1,500 at 4–8 and 1,800 at 9–13. The alcohol advice is simply to drink less, with no numeric limit, and to avoid alcohol entirely during pregnancy, in recovery from alcohol use disorder, for anyone who can't control how much they drink, and with medicines or medical conditions that interact with it. Its consumer graphic is a new food pyramid. The 2020–2025 edition, which older course materials may still teach, used MyPlate (fruits, vegetables, grains, protein foods and dairy). It limited added sugars and saturated fat to less than 10% of calories each from age 2, ruled out added sugars before age 2, capped sodium at 2,300 mg, and told adults who drink to stop at 2 drinks a day for men and 1 for women. On a Nutrition Facts label, 5% of the Daily Value or less per serving is low and 20% or more is high. Aim low for saturated fat, sodium and added sugars, and high for fiber, vitamin D, calcium, iron and potassium.
points: 2025–2030 targets: "eat real food" · protein 1.2–1.6 g/kg/day · whole grains 2–4 servings · dairy 3, vegetables 3 and fruit 2 servings on a 2,000-calorie pattern
2025–2030 limits: saturated fat ≤10% of calories · no added sugar recommended (≤10 g per meal) · sodium <2,300 mg from age 14 · drink less alcohol
2020–2025 limits: added sugars and saturated fat each <10% of calories from age 2 · no added sugars under 2 · sodium <2,300 mg · alcohol ≤2 drinks a day for men, ≤1 for women
MyPlate (2020–2025): fruits, vegetables, grains, protein foods and dairy, with half the plate fruits and vegetables
Label rule: 5% DV or less is low and 20% or more is high; the serving size isn't a recommendation

topics.title: Feeding children and teens, and eating disorders
topics.eli5: Kids are building their bodies, so they need nutrient-packed food, patient chances to try new foods and as little added sugar as possible.
topics.detail: The 2025–2030 Dietary Guidelines include advice for each life stage. Infants should get only breast milk for about the first 6 months, or iron-fortified formula when breast milk isn't available, and breastfeeding can continue as long as mother and child want, to 2 years or beyond. Breastfed infants, and infants who drink less than 32 ounces of formula a day, need a daily 400 IU vitamin D supplement starting shortly after birth. Solid foods start at about 6 months, including potentially allergenic foods such as eggs, nut butters, shellfish and wheat. Infants at high risk of peanut allergy may start peanut foods as early as 4–6 months under a clinician's guidance. Formula stops at 12 months, when whole milk can start. Added sugars should be avoided from birth through age 4, and for ages 5–10 no amount is recommended. Full-fat dairy helps children meet their energy needs and supports brain development, and caffeinated drinks should be avoided. It may take 8 to 10 exposures before a young child is willing to try a new food, so caregivers should keep offering foods and eat well themselves. Adolescents (11–18) grow fast and need more energy, protein, calcium and iron, especially girls because of menstruation. They also need calcium and vitamin D to build peak bone mass, and should limit sugary and energy drinks. Eating disorders often begin in adolescence. Anorexia nervosa involves severe restriction and an intense fear of gaining weight, bulimia nervosa involves binge eating followed by purging or other compensating behavior, and binge-eating disorder involves repeated binges without purging. All three are serious mental illnesses that need professional treatment. Warning signs include rapid weight change, secretive eating, obsessive dieting or exercise, and a distorted body image.
points: 0–6 months: breast milk only (or iron-fortified formula) · 400 IU of vitamin D a day for breastfed infants and those drinking under 32 oz of formula a day
About 6 months: start solids, including common allergens · 12 months: stop formula and start whole milk
Added sugars: avoid from birth to age 4, and none recommended at ages 5–10 (2025–2030)
8–10 exposures before a young child may be willing to try a new food
Teens need more calcium, vitamin D, iron and protein, and should limit sugary and energy drinks
Eating disorders: anorexia (restriction) · bulimia (binge, then purge) · binge-eating disorder (binges without purging)

topics.title: Body weight, chronic disease and lifestyle
topics.eli5: Most of the diseases that kill Americans grow slowly out of everyday habits. That's good news, because everyday habits can also slow or stop them.
topics.detail: Chronic diseases cause most U.S. deaths and most health care spending. In CDC's 2024 data, the leading causes of death were heart disease, cancer and unintentional injuries, followed by stroke, chronic lower respiratory disease, Alzheimer's disease and diabetes. Body mass index (BMI) is weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared (or 703 × pounds ÷ inches²). For adults, under 18.5 is underweight, 18.5 to under 25 is healthy, 25 to under 30 is overweight and 30 or more is obesity. BMI is a screening tool, not a diagnosis, because it doesn't measure body fat directly; waist size adds information about belly fat. Children and teens (2–19) use BMI-for-age percentiles: below the 5th is underweight, the 5th to below the 85th is healthy, the 85th to below the 95th is overweight, and the 95th or above is obesity. Body weight reflects energy balance: calories eaten against calories burned through resting metabolism, digestion and activity. Cardiovascular disease usually starts with atherosclerosis, plaque that narrows and stiffens the arteries. A blocked coronary artery causes a heart attack, and a blocked or burst blood vessel in the brain causes a stroke. The American Heart Association classes blood pressure as normal (below 120/80), elevated (120–129 systolic with diastolic below 80), stage 1 hypertension (130–139 or 80–89) and stage 2 (140 or higher, or 90 or higher). In type 1 diabetes, about 5–10% of cases, an autoimmune reaction stops insulin production. In type 2, about 90–95% of cases, the body doesn't use insulin well; it develops over years and is increasingly diagnosed in young people. CDC says about 8 in 10 people with prediabetes don't know they have it. Cancer risk rises with tobacco, alcohol, obesity, inactivity, too much sun and some infections; vaccines prevent HPV and hepatitis B, which can cause cancer. Modifiable risk factors are the lever. The American Heart Association's Life's Essential 8 are: eat better, be more active, quit tobacco, get healthy sleep, manage weight, control cholesterol, manage blood sugar and manage blood pressure.
points: Adult BMI: <18.5 underweight · 18.5–24.9 healthy · 25–29.9 overweight · 30+ obesity
Ages 2–19, BMI-for-age percentile: <5th · 5th to <85th · 85th to <95th · ≥95th
Blood pressure: normal <120/80 · elevated 120–129 and <80 · stage 1 130–139 or 80–89 · stage 2 ≥140 or ≥90
A1C: normal <5.7% · prediabetes 5.7–6.4% · diabetes ≥6.5% (fasting glucose ≥126 mg/dL)
Life's Essential 8: diet, activity, tobacco, sleep, weight, cholesterol, blood sugar, blood pressure
Worked BMI: 70 kg ÷ (1.75 m)² = 70 ÷ 3.06 ≈ 22.9 (healthy)

topics.title: Infectious disease, immunity and sexual health
topics.eli5: Germs need a path from one person to the next. Handwashing, vaccines and condoms break that path, and your immune system cleans up whatever gets through.
topics.detail: Infectious diseases are caused by pathogens: bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites and prions. The chain of infection has six links: the infectious agent, a reservoir where it lives, a portal of exit, a mode of transmission, a portal of entry and a susceptible host. Transmission is either direct (touch, sexual contact, droplets from coughs and sneezes) or indirect (particles that stay in the air, contaminated food, water or objects, and vectors such as mosquitoes and ticks). Breaking any link stops the spread, which is why handwashing, cleaning, vaccination, safe food handling and staying home when sick work. The immune system has innate defenses (skin, mucous membranes, stomach acid, inflammation, fever, and white blood cells such as phagocytes) and adaptive defenses: B cells make antibodies, T cells destroy infected cells, and memory cells make the response faster next time. Active immunity comes from infection or vaccination and lasts. Passive immunity, such as the antibodies a baby gets through the placenta or breast milk, is borrowed and temporary. When enough people are immune, community (herd) immunity protects those who can't be vaccinated. Antibiotics treat bacterial infections but not viruses, and overusing them breeds resistant bacteria. Sexually transmitted infections are common and often cause no symptoms. Bacterial STIs such as chlamydia, gonorrhea and syphilis can be cured with antibiotics. Viral STIs such as HPV, genital herpes, HIV and hepatitis B have no cure, though medicines can control HIV and herpes and help some people with chronic hepatitis B. HPV itself has no treatment, but doctors can treat the genital warts and precancers it causes, and about 9 in 10 HPV infections clear on their own within two years. Vaccines prevent HPV and hepatitis B. Prevention includes abstinence, consistent condom use, mutual monogamy with a tested partner, vaccination and regular testing.
points: Chain of infection: agent → reservoir → portal of exit → mode of transmission → portal of entry → susceptible host
Innate immunity (general and fast) vs adaptive immunity (specific, with memory)
Active immunity (infection or vaccine) lasts · passive immunity (a mother's antibodies) is temporary
Antibiotics treat bacteria, not viruses such as colds and flu
Curable bacterial STIs: chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis · viral STIs with no cure: HPV, herpes, HIV, hepatitis B (medicines control some, and most HPV clears on its own)

topics.title: Substance use: alcohol, nicotine, cannabis and opioids
topics.eli5: Drugs change how the brain's reward and self-control systems work, and a teen brain that's still being built is easier to change for good, so starting late or never is the safest bet.
topics.detail: NIDA defines addiction as a chronic, relapsing disorder of compulsive drug seeking and use despite harmful consequences. It changes the brain circuits for reward, stress and self-control, and it's preventable and treatable. Adolescents are especially vulnerable because the prefrontal cortex, which handles judgment and impulse control, keeps developing into adulthood, and early use strongly predicts later problems. Risk factors include early aggressive behavior, little parental supervision, easy access to drugs, poverty and friends who use. Protective factors include involved parents, self-control, success at school and school anti-drug policies, and genes account for an estimated 40–60% of addiction risk. A U.S. standard drink holds 14 grams (0.6 fl oz) of pure alcohol: 12 oz of 5% beer, 5 oz of 12% wine or 1.5 oz of 80-proof (40%) spirits. NIAAA defines binge drinking as a pattern that brings blood alcohol concentration to 0.08% or higher, typically 4 or more drinks for women or 5 or more for men in about 2 hours. Alcohol is a depressant that impairs judgment and coordination, and heavy use damages the liver and heart and raises cancer risk. Nicotine is highly addictive and harms the developing adolescent brain. E-cigarettes are still the most used tobacco product among U.S. middle and high school students: 5.2%, about 1.44 million students, in the 2025 National Youth Tobacco Survey, ahead of nicotine pouches. THC, the main psychoactive chemical in cannabis, can impair memory, attention and coordination, and many of today's products are far stronger than in the past. Opioids (prescription painkillers, heroin and illegally made fentanyl) slow breathing and are involved in most U.S. overdose deaths; naloxone can reverse an opioid overdose, though someone should still call 911 and stay with the person until help arrives. Prevention focuses on delaying first use, refusal skills, honest information and strong ties to family and school.
points: Standard drink = 14 g of alcohol: 12 oz beer (5%) · 5 oz wine (12%) · 1.5 oz spirits (40%)
Binge drinking: BAC ≥0.08%, typically 4+ drinks for women or 5+ for men in about 2 hours
Addiction: a chronic, relapsing brain disorder that's preventable and treatable
E-cigarettes: the most used youth tobacco product (5.2% of students in 2025)
Naloxone reverses an opioid overdose (still call 911)
Protective factors: involved parents, self-control, connection to school, delaying first use

keyFacts.value: Precontemplation (no plan to change in the next ~6 months) → contemplation (within ~6 months) → preparation (within ~1 month) → action → maintenance (6+ months)

keyFacts.value: Fight-or-flight: adrenaline and cortisol · general adaptation syndrome: alarm → resistance → exhaustion

keyFacts.value: 33% of high school students felt persistently sad or hopeless (43% of girls, 24% of boys) · 14% seriously considered suicide

keyFacts.value: Ages 3–5: active all day (about 3 h of play) · ages 6–17: 60+ min daily, with vigorous, muscle- and bone-strengthening each on 3+ days a week

keyFacts.value: 150–300 min moderate or 75–150 min vigorous a week + muscle-strengthening on 2+ days
keyFacts.note: 1 vigorous minute counts about the same as 2 moderate minutes; older adults add balance training; pregnancy and postpartum: 150+ min moderate; bouts of any length count

keyFacts.value: METs: moderate 3.0–5.9, vigorous 6.0+ · 0–10 scale: moderate 5–6, vigorous starts at 7–8 · talk test: moderate = can talk but not sing

keyFacts.value: Max ≈ 220 − age · moderate ≈ 50–70% of max · vigorous ≈ 70–85% · normal resting 60–100 bpm
keyFacts.note: Age 30: max 190, moderate ≈ 95–133 bpm; other sources use slightly different percentages

keyFacts.value: Health-related: cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility, body composition · skill-related: agility, balance, coordination, power, reaction time, speed

keyFacts.value: Carbohydrate 4 · protein 4 · fat 9 · alcohol 7

keyFacts.label: AMDRs
keyFacts.value: Adults: carbohydrate 45–65% · fat 20–35% · protein 10–35% of calories

keyFacts.label: Vitamins and minerals
keyFacts.value: Fat-soluble: A, D, E, K · water-soluble: C and the B vitamins · calcium + vitamin D for bones · iron for blood (anemia)

tasks: Discuss your course planning tool report with your instructor, and ask which Dietary Guidelines edition the course materials follow.
Skim how the course materials are organized and look for a pre-assessment. If there is one, take it cold to find your weakest competencies.
Start a one-page numbers sheet using this guide's key facts.

plan.focus: Wellness models, determinants and behavior change
tasks: Learn your course's list of wellness dimensions (SAMHSA lists eight), the five social-determinant domains and the five stages of change.
Write one modifiable and one non-modifiable risk factor for heart disease, then one SMART goal of your own.

plan.focus: Mental and emotional health, stress and sleep
tasks: Cover what influences mental and emotional wellness, eustress vs distress, the stress response and the three stages of general adaptation syndrome.
Learn healthy vs unhealthy coping, the warning signs that call for help (and 988), sleep hours by age and sleep hygiene.

plan.focus: Social and emotional learning and social wellness
tasks: Learn the CASEL 5 with two example behaviors for each, plus the four settings.
Review communication styles, conflict resolution, bullying and refusal skills.
Write 10 short school or family scenarios and name the CASEL competency each one shows.
Memorize the guidelines for ages 3–5, 6–17, adults, older adults and pregnancy.
List the benefits of activity for children and adults, and remember that bouts of any length count.
Learn the five health-related and six skill-related components, FITT and the training principles.
Practice METs, the 0–10 scale, the talk test and target heart rate math for ages 20, 40 and 60.
Learn the six nutrient classes, calories per gram, the AMDRs, fiber, complete vs incomplete proteins and the types of fat.
Cover fat- vs water-soluble vitamins and key minerals (calcium, vitamin D, iron, sodium, potassium), then do five calorie calculations.

plan.focus: The Dietary Guidelines and food labels
tasks: Make a two-column table: the 2025–2030 targets and limits next to the 2020–2025 limits and MyPlate.
Read three real Nutrition Facts labels with the 5%/20% rule.
Learn the infant feeding milestones, the added-sugar and sodium limits by age, the 8–10 exposures a new food may need, and teens' calcium and iron needs.
Cover anorexia, bulimia and binge-eating disorder: their main features and warning signs.
Learn BMI for adults and for children, energy balance, atherosclerosis, and heart attack vs stroke.
Learn the blood pressure categories, the diabetes types and A1C ranges, cancer risk factors and Life's Essential 8.
Learn the chain of infection, innate vs adaptive and active vs passive immunity, what antibiotics can and can't treat, and STIs.
Cover addiction and why teens are at higher risk, standard drinks and binge drinking, nicotine and vaping, cannabis, opioids and naloxone.
Do this guide's practice questions and the course pre-assessment, if there is one, then review every miss by competency.
Drill the numbers sheet until you can write it from memory.
Set up an elevated external webcam and speakers, run WGU's System Check on the exam computer, then schedule the OA.
Clear the desk, close other programs, and keep your hands in view; no headphones.
Before answering, check the age group and the key word (most, first, best) in every question.

practice.q: A student notices that a classmate who just moved from another country is eating lunch alone, and imagines how lonely and out of place that must feel. Which CASEL competency is the student showing?
practice.why: Social awareness is understanding other people's perspectives and feeling empathy for them, including people with different backgrounds. Self-awareness would mean noticing the student's own feelings, and self-management would mean regulating them. Responsible decision-making is choosing what to do next, such as inviting the classmate to sit together, which would also draw on relationship skills.

practice.q: A teenager is furious at a referee's call. They take three slow breaths, count to ten and walk to the bench instead of yelling. Which CASEL competency is this?
practice.why: Self-management is regulating your emotions, thoughts and behavior, including handling strong feelings and controlling impulses, which is exactly what the breathing and counting do. Noticing the anger in the first place would be self-awareness. Social awareness is about understanding others, relationship skills are about communicating and resolving conflict with them, and responsible decision-making is about weighing choices and consequences.

practice.q: A smoker says, "I know I should quit, and I'm thinking about doing it in the next few months, but I'm not ready to set a date." Which stage of change is this?
practice.why: In the transtheoretical model, contemplation means seriously thinking about changing within roughly the next six months without having committed to a plan. Precontemplation means not intending to change in the next six months, preparation means planning to act soon (usually within a month) with concrete steps, and action means the behavior has recently changed. Support works best when it matches the stage, such as weighing pros and cons with someone in contemplation.

practice.q: After months of nonstop work and caregiving stress, a person's body can no longer keep up its heightened response: they're worn out, keep getting sick and feel unable to cope. Which stage of Selye's general adaptation syndrome is this?
practice.why: General adaptation syndrome has three stages: alarm (the fight-or-flight surge of adrenaline and cortisol), resistance (the body stays on high alert and tries to adapt) and exhaustion (resources run down after prolonged stress, raising the risk of illness, burnout and depression). Recovery isn't one of Selye's three stages, although rest and good coping help the body return to normal.

practice.q: Which weekly plan meets the Physical Activity Guidelines for a healthy 12-year-old?
choices: 30 minutes of moderate activity on school days only, with vigorous and muscle-strengthening activity saved for weekend sports
60 or more minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity every day, including vigorous, muscle-strengthening and bone-strengthening activity on at least 3 days each
150 minutes of moderate activity spread across the week, plus muscle-strengthening activity for all major muscle groups on 2 days
About 3 hours a day of light activity, such as slow walking and casual play, with no moderate or vigorous activity
practice.answer: 60 or more minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity every day, including vigorous, muscle-strengthening and bone-strengthening activity on at least 3 days each
practice.why: Children and adolescents ages 6–17 need 60 minutes or more of moderate-to-vigorous activity daily, mostly aerobic, with vigorous activity, muscle-strengthening (such as climbing or push-ups) and bone-strengthening (such as jumping or running) each on at least 3 days a week. 30 minutes on school days falls well short of 60 minutes every day, 150 minutes a week plus 2 strength days is the adult guideline, and light activity alone, however long, doesn't count toward the daily 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity (about 3 hours a day of activity at any intensity is the target for preschoolers, ages 3–5).

practice.q: Which weekly routine meets both parts of the adult guidelines, aerobic and muscle-strengthening?
choices: Brisk walking for 20 minutes on 5 days, with no strength training
Full-body strength training on 4 days, with no aerobic activity
Jogging for 25 minutes on 3 days, plus full-body strength training on 2 days
A 10-minute walk on Saturday and Sunday, plus stretching once a week
practice.answer: Jogging for 25 minutes on 3 days, plus full-body strength training on 2 days
practice.why: Adults need 150–300 minutes of moderate or 75–150 minutes of vigorous aerobic activity a week (1 vigorous minute counts about the same as 2 moderate minutes), plus muscle-strengthening for all major muscle groups on 2 or more days. Jogging 25 minutes on 3 days is 75 vigorous minutes, and the 2 strength days complete the guideline. Walking 20 minutes on 5 days is only 100 moderate minutes, strength training alone misses the aerobic part, and the weekend routine falls far short of both, although any activity beats none.

practice.q: Using the American Heart Association's estimate, what is the moderate-intensity target heart rate range for a 30-year-old?
practice.why: Estimated maximum heart rate is about 220 minus age, so 220 − 30 = 190 bpm. Moderate intensity is roughly 50–70% of maximum: 0.50 × 190 = 95 and 0.70 × 190 = 133. 133–162 bpm (70–85%) is the vigorous range, 60–100 bpm is a normal resting heart rate, and 190 is the estimated maximum itself. The talk test (you can talk but not sing) is a quick check that doesn't need a pulse count.

practice.q: A snack bar has 8 g of fat, 20 g of carbohydrate and 6 g of protein. About how many calories does it have?
practice.why: Fat has about 9 calories per gram, and carbohydrate and protein about 4 each: (8 × 9) + (20 × 4) + (6 × 4) = 72 + 80 + 24 = 176 calories. 136 counts every gram at 4 calories, 306 counts every gram at 9, and 34 just adds up the grams. Fat supplies 72 of the 176 calories, about 41%.

practice.q: Why are adolescents especially vulnerable to developing a substance use disorder?
choices: Their livers break down alcohol and drugs faster than adults' livers do
Addiction risk is decided entirely by genes, which switch on in the teen years
Their prefrontal cortex, which handles judgment and impulse control, is still developing
Teens can't become physically dependent on nicotine or cannabis
practice.answer: Their prefrontal cortex, which handles judgment and impulse control, is still developing
practice.why: NIDA explains that the brain keeps developing into adulthood and the prefrontal cortex, which handles judgment and self-control, matures last, so teens take more risks and drugs can change a brain that's still developing. Early use also strongly predicts later problems. Genes matter (an estimated 40–60% of addiction risk) but don't decide it alone; peers, family and protective factors such as involved parents count too. Teens can become dependent on nicotine and cannabis, and liver speed isn't what makes them vulnerable.

practice.q: Under the Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2025–2030, which statement about added sugars is correct?
choices: Keep added sugars below 10% of daily calories, starting at age 2
No amount of added sugar is recommended, and one meal should contain no more than 10 grams
Up to 50 grams a day of added sugar fits a healthy diet for most adults
Only sugar-sweetened drinks count as added sugar; sugars added to packaged foods don't
practice.answer: No amount of added sugar is recommended, and one meal should contain no more than 10 grams
practice.why: The 2025–2030 edition says no amount of added sugars or non-nutritive sweeteners is recommended, caps a single meal at 10 grams of added sugar, and says to avoid added sugars entirely for young children. The under-10%-of-calories limit from age 2 (about 50 grams on 2,000 calories) is the 2020–2025 rule, which older course materials may still teach. Added sugars include sugars and syrups added to any food, not just drinks; the sugars naturally in fruit and plain milk don't count.

practice.q: A 9-year-old's BMI-for-age falls at the 88th percentile on CDC's growth charts. Which category is that?
practice.why: For ages 2–19, CDC uses BMI-for-age percentiles: below the 5th is underweight, the 5th to below the 85th is healthy weight, the 85th to below the 95th is overweight, and the 95th or above is obesity. A child's BMI is compared with others of the same age and sex because body fat changes as kids grow, so the adult cutoffs of 25 and 30 don't apply.

practice.q: An adult's blood pressure reads 134/78 mm Hg. Using the American Heart Association's categories, how is it classified?
practice.why: Stage 1 hypertension is a systolic reading of 130–139 or a diastolic reading of 80–89, and one number in range is enough, so 134 qualifies even though 78 is below 80. Elevated is 120–129 systolic with diastolic below 80, normal is below 120/80, and stage 2 starts at 140 systolic or 90 diastolic. A diagnosis relies on repeated readings, not a single one.

choices: The body doesn't use insulin well; it develops over years, is linked to excess weight and inactivity, and makes up about 90–95% of diagnosed cases
An autoimmune reaction stops the body from making insulin, and it's usually diagnosed in childhood or young adulthood
High blood sugar that first appears during pregnancy and usually goes away after delivery
A brief drop in blood sugar caused by skipping a meal
practice.answer: The body doesn't use insulin well; it develops over years, is linked to excess weight and inactivity, and makes up about 90–95% of diagnosed cases
practice.why: Type 2 diabetes involves insulin resistance, builds gradually, and is increasingly diagnosed in young people; healthy eating, activity and weight management can prevent or delay it. The autoimmune description is type 1 (about 5–10% of cases, with no known prevention), the pregnancy description is gestational diabetes, and a skipped-meal drop is low blood sugar (hypoglycemia), not diabetes.

practice.q: Which counts as one U.S. standard drink, about 14 grams of pure alcohol?
choices: 5 fl oz of wine at 12% alcohol
12 fl oz of wine at 12% alcohol
1.5 fl oz of beer at 5% alcohol
practice.answer: 5 fl oz of wine at 12% alcohol
practice.why: A standard drink is 12 fl oz of regular beer (5%), 5 fl oz of wine (12%) or 1.5 fl oz of 80-proof (40%) spirits, each holding about 0.6 fl oz of pure alcohol. Twelve ounces of wine is more than two drinks, 1.5 oz of beer is a sip, and 8 oz of 80-proof liquor is more than five drinks. The sizes matter because binge drinking (BAC of 0.08% or more, typically 4+ drinks for women or 5+ for men in about 2 hours) is counted in standard drinks, not glasses.

practice.q: Which sexually transmitted infection can be cured with antibiotics?
practice.why: Chlamydia, gonorrhea and syphilis are bacterial and can be cured with the right antibiotics, although you can be reinfected. HPV, HIV and herpes are viruses with no cure, and antibiotics don't work on viruses: medicines control HIV and herpes, doctors can treat the warts and precancers HPV causes, and most HPV infections clear on their own. Vaccines prevent HPV and hepatitis B, and because many STIs cause no symptoms, regular testing is part of prevention.

pitfalls: Mixing up guideline editions. The Dietary Guidelines changed in January 2026. A question that uses MyPlate or a 10%-of-calories limit on added sugar is drawing on the 2020–2025 edition, so learn both sets of numbers.
Using adult numbers for children. Children have their own rules for activity (60 minutes daily at 6–17), sleep (9–12 hours at 6–12, 8–10 for teens), sodium and BMI. Read the age in every question.

Blurring the CASEL competencies. Noticing your own feelings is self-awareness, controlling them is self-management, understanding someone else's is social awareness, working things out with others (including resisting negative peer pressure) is relationship skills, and weighing the consequences of a choice is responsible decision-making.
Calorie math slips. Fat is 9 calories per gram, not 4, and alcohol is 7 even though it isn't a nutrient.

Intensity mix-ups. Moderate is 3–5.9 METs, 5–6 on the 0–10 scale or about 50–70% of maximum heart rate. Vigorous is 6+ METs, 7–8 and up, or about 70–85%. Talk test: if you can talk but not sing, it's moderate.
Treating BMI as a diagnosis. BMI is a screening tool, and children use percentiles for their age and sex, not the adult cutoffs of 25 and 30.
Antibiotics for viruses. Antibiotics treat bacterial infections such as strep throat or chlamydia, not colds, flu or other viruses, and overuse breeds resistant bacteria.

Calling addiction a choice. NIDA defines it as a chronic, relapsing brain disorder that's preventable and treatable. Know the risk and protective factors, and describe addiction in NIDA's terms rather than as a moral failing.

Proctoring surprises. A laptop's built-in webcam doesn't meet WGU's requirement (the external webcam must be elevated), headphones aren't allowed, and Chromebooks, Linux, Windows on Arm or S Mode, virtual machines and tablets can't run proctored OAs. Set up an elevated external webcam and run WGU's System Check before exam day.

Buying "actual exam" banks. Sites selling supposed C458 exam questions show up all over search results. Using WGU assessment content found online violates WGU's academic integrity policy, and those sets may teach outdated guidelines.

caveats: This guide is study material for a college course, not medical, nutrition or mental-health advice. For your own health decisions, talk with a qualified health professional, and in a crisis call or text 988.

No readable student reports were available. Reddit couldn't be opened for this research and the community notes held only one thread title, so the OA's question count, time limit, question types, passing score and topic weights are all unknown.

Guidance changed recently. The Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2025–2030 (Jan 2026) replaced the 2020–2025 edition. It uses a food pyramid graphic and doesn't mention MyPlate, replaces the numeric alcohol limits with advice to drink less, and replaces the 10%-of-calories added-sugar limit with advice that no amount is recommended (and no more than 10 grams in a meal). Course materials often lag, so the OA may still test the older numbers; this guide gives both. HHS is also preparing a 2027 supplement to the Physical Activity Guidelines.

The competency wording comes from WGU's Cybersecurity and Information Assurance guidebook (catalog 202610), which lists the same C458 course, because the BSCS guidebook PDF is image-only. The course's own textbook or materials couldn't be checked from public sources, so its terms and lists (for example, how many wellness dimensions it names, or which heart-rate percentages it uses) may differ from this guide's.
Statistics such as the 2025 youth survey results, the 2024 causes-of-death ranking and youth tobacco figures change every year or two, and the course may quote older numbers.
The practice questions are original, written from the official competencies and federal guidance, so they can't be matched to the real exam's difficulty or style.
